source.title: Monotonicity and Double Descent in Uncertainty Estimation with Gaussian Processes
source.authors: Liam Hodgkinson; C. van der Heide; Fred Roosta; Michael W. Mahoney

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary document are present
record.tranche_reason: Tests double-descent behavior in Gaussian-process posterior predictive losses using input-dimension sweeps, rather than the original deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's double-descent results are for posterior predictive losses and their dependence on input dimension. Its marginal-likelihood results are a different metric, not test-error results. Values for the plotted curves are not numerically tabulated; descriptions in the text determine the reported states. The paper cites other studies' double-descent findings, which are not recorded as results here.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps input dimension d at fixed n in GP regression, which for the linear kernel is Bayesian linear regression with d parameters. It reports posterior-predictive test losses (PPL2) on synthetic and real data, with and without optimal regularization, so its own results bear on whether risk rises and falls again around d≈n and whether tuned regularization removes the peak. This is a new (Bayesian uncertainty-metric) setting, not the originals' method.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors find increasing temperature mitigates the double-descent singularity, recommend against PPL2 as an uncertainty metric because of the cold posterior effect, and say tuning by marginal likelihood negates the curse of dimensionality.
record.recipe_differences: Studies Gaussian processes and posterior predictive losses over input dimension, rather than deep-network model size, training epochs, or test error in the original settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior depends on kernel (linear versus Gaussian), temperature/coldness, and regularization choice; optimizing λ for PPL2 yields monotone decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Bayes free energy (marginal likelihood) at optimal λ* decreases monotonically with input dimension (Theorem 1, Figs. 1, 2, 6, 8). It rises at large d for fixed λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under empirical-Bayes tuning, marginal-likelihood performance of GPs improves monotonically with input dimension, unlike cross-validation losses.

fits_no_version.finding: Free energy shows 'double-ascent' under large prior misspecification (Fig. 12). It is non-monotone for ill-conditioned inputs at low temperature (Fig. 14). Adding iid Gaussian covariates keeps monotone decay, but repeated or zero-padded covariates do not (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Monotonicity of marginal likelihood in input dimension depends on prior specification and on input whitening or conditioning.

fits_no_version.finding: Bayes free energy can worsen with more data when d grows sublinearly in n (Fig. 15).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More data can hurt marginal likelihood when input dimension scales slower than n.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, 2023
record.problems: The results concern Gaussian processes and input dimension, not deep-network size, epochs, or sample-size sweeps. The theoretical claims rely on specified data and kernel assumptions. Most empirical curves are presented as figures rather than numerical tables, and the paper itself cautions that input dimension and model complexity should not be conflated.

untested.parts: No test-error curves over sample size near the threshold. The Fig. 15 data-scaling result is for Bayes free energy, not test error.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Label noise in the data as the driver of the peak; triple or multiple descent in test loss.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count. Authors only caution that input dimension is not model complexity.

missing.what: PPL2 double-descent curves on real datasets (CT Slices, MNIST, CIFAR10) at λ* and at fixed λ with γ=0.1, matching the synthetic curves
Optimally tempered PPNLL under the linear kernel increases monotonically with dimension at fixed µ and is flat when optimized in both γ and µ; no double descent

record.verdict_notes: The complexity axis is input dimension, which equals parameter count only for the linear kernel; the authors stress this caveat themselves. The paper's definition of double descent (a single global maximum, then monotone decrease) excludes multiple descent. All curves are figure-only; states rest on the authors' descriptions. Free-energy results concern a different metric (marginal likelihood), not test error, so they are kept out of version verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and peaks near the training-set interpolation size.
Increasing training sample size near the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Does not test generalization across all model classes; its sweeps use GP input dimension, not a broad capacity sweep across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

Does not establish that label noise or variance drives the peak, test multiple/triple descent, or test all regularization choices. It reports temperature and regularization effects on GP predictive-loss curves.
Does not re-express the curves using an effective parameter count or test whether that turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Linear-kernel PPL2 under varying temperature and regularization
relationships.reason: Colder posteriors (weaker effective regularization) induce the peak, and warmer ones mitigate it (R2). Optimizing λ for PPL2 removes the peak, giving monotone decay (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Colder posteriors induced the peak and warmer posteriors mitigated it, while optimizing λ removed it and yielded monotone PPL2 decay.
